metadata.title: PISA 2018 Results (Volume IV): Are Students Smart about Money?

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This volume reports PISA 2018 results based on a complex multi-stage sampling design of schools and students within participating education systems. The report indicates that school-principal questionnaire responses are weighted to be proportionate to the number of 15-year-olds enrolled in the school, implying the use of sampling/analysis weights for questionnaire-based indicators. For student performance indicators (including financial literacy), the publication follows PISA’s standard international reporting approach, which is designed to produce representative estimates for each country/economy while accounting for the survey design. The excerpt provided does not specify the exact student weight variable names or replicate-weight method (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so the precise weighting implementation details cannot be extracted from the provided text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This is an OECD/PISA results volume that reports descriptive and comparative statistics (e.g., mean scores, proficiency shares, and score differences) rather than training or evaluating predictive ML models on student-level data. The provided excerpt does not document a specific plausible-values (PV) handling strategy or a missing-data handling procedure for any PV-based achievement modelling, so PV/missing-data treatment cannot be extracted from the text shown. This represents a reporting gap for the purposes of PV/missing-data metadata extraction, even though PISA typically uses PVs for cognitive achievement scales.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The financial literacy assessment in PISA 2018 was administered as an optional one-hour module to a subsample of students in participating countries/economies. The excerpt specifies that the financial literacy assessment was conducted in Australia, Brazil, Bulgaria, Canada, Chile, Estonia, Finland, Georgia, Indonesia, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Peru, Poland, Portugal, the Russian Federation, Serbia, the Slovak Republic, Spain and the United States. The report targets 15-year-old students (aged 15 years 3 months to 16 years 2 months) enrolled in school and having completed at least 6 years of formal schooling, with an overall exclusion rate required to remain below 5% (and reported as below 2% in 28 systems and below 5% in 63 systems). The provided excerpt does not specify additional analytic exclusions beyond the PISA standard exclusion criteria and the optional-module subsampling.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD volume reports PISA 2018 financial literacy results (optional assessment) for 15-year-old students across 21 countries/economies that administered the financial literacy module. The assessment is delivered as part of the broader PISA 2018 computer-based testing (with paper-based options in some systems) and uses a one-hour financial literacy module administered to a subsample of students alongside core PISA assessments. Results are presented as mean financial literacy scores, proficiency-level distributions (Levels 1–5), and score differences, including relative performance after accounting for mathematics and reading performance. The executive summary reports that Estonia has the highest mean financial literacy score, that about 85% of students across OECD countries/economies reach at least Level 2, and that around 10% reach Level 5. It also documents associations between financial literacy and gender, socio-economic status, immigrant background, and several money-related behaviours/attitudes, while emphasizing that these are descriptive/associational patterns within PISA’s cross-sectional design.
